name: Weekly Review v2
description: Consolidated weekly review organized BY PROJECT, built to be trusted at a glance. The pre-meeting notes/deck are the GROUND TRUTH for status; the meeting audio is a rougher secondary source used mainly for questions, feedback and decisions. Every item is grounded and, when it comes from audio and is uncertain, visibly flagged so the reader verifies only the shaky 25%, not the whole thing. For each project it captures Progress, Blockers, Questions raised, Feedback, and Next steps; then rolls up open questions and cross-cutting feedback, and ends with an explicit list of what was uncertain. Merges mentions of the same project under different names into one entry.

sections.title: Week Of
sections.instruction: The week or date range this review covers, plus the meeting date. Use ONLY dates actually stated in the notes or spoken in the meeting — never invent or guess a year, month, or day. If a date was clearly stated relative to the meeting (e.g. 'next Tuesday'), you may keep the relative phrase.

sections.title: Projects
sections.instruction:
Organize the entire review BY PROJECT, not by team or speaker. GROUND EVERYTHING: the pre-meeting notes and slide/PDF deck are the reliable source of truth for what happened; the meeting transcript is a rougher secondary source. When the transcript disagrees with the notes on a fact (a number, a name, a status), TRUST THE NOTES and do not repeat the transcript's version. Never invent, 'correct', or guess a proper noun (project, product, person, place); if the audio clearly garbled one and the notes don't cover it, keep your best guess and append '[?]'. Preserve every exact number, percentage, count, and date VERBATIM from the notes (e.g. '226/316 SOF', '387 devices', '~80%') — do not round or approximate them away. Every figure stated in the notes is REQUIRED content: if the notes say it, the output must contain it. Dropping a number to keep prose smooth is a failure.

Several teams report each week and often discuss the SAME project using different names, nicknames, or phrasing. Recognize aliases and MERGE them into ONE entry — cluster by what is actually being worked on. A strong signal two candidates are one project: they share a blocker, question, or action. Scan the WHOLE transcript and notes first, build one list of distinct projects, and fold every alias and later revisit into a single entry. Never split one project across teams. Do NOT attribute lines to named internal speakers ('Backend said…', 'Priya said…'); keep a role or client/PIC name ONLY when it is part of the factual content ('the client asked', 'waiting on Kak Ros', 'sent to Justin'). For each distinct project create a '### <Project name>' subsection using the clearest consistent name. A block of work with NO stated project name is STILL a project — never drop it: if a stretch of the notes or audio describes real work (components like a 'Node' and a 'Master', a subsystem, a deliverable, a pile of commits) but nobody gives it a project name, create a subsection anyway using the most descriptive label you can build from its own contents (e.g. the component names) and append '[?]' to that invented label. Treat every separate notes document or top-level heading as its own project unless it clearly continues another. Order projects strictly from most-discussed to least-discussed. Under each project include these headings IN THIS ORDER, and include a heading ONLY when it has real content — omit any that would be empty:

(1) '**Progress this week**' — a paragraph of concrete outcomes ONLY: work ACTUALLY finished, shipped, or moved forward THIS WEEK, taken primarily from the notes/deck. Keep the exact figures. Do NOT restate goals. Do NOT report something as done if it is only planned, promised, or agreed for later — that is a NEXT STEP. Blend every team's update into one coherent paragraph.

(2) '**Blockers & risks**' — ONLY if the project genuinely has one. Anything stuck, at risk, waiting on a decision, or waiting on another team/person (waiting on someone else IS a blocker), plus what is needed to clear it. If none, OMIT the heading — never write 'None' or 'N/A'.

(3) '**Questions raised**' — ONLY if at least one question was asked about this project. A markdown table '| Question | Answer / Resolution |'. One question per row, paraphrased clearly. In the Answer cell, summarize the answer given; if no answer was given, write exactly 'Open — not answered'. Cite the transcript line range for each in the Answer cell (e.g. '(lines 52-63)'). Omit the heading and table if no question was raised.

(4) '**Feedback & comments**' — ONLY if at least one comment was made. A bulleted list: every concern, critique, praise, suggestion, request, or directive aimed at this project — one concrete point per bullet, paraphrased, with a line-range cite. Do NOT restate status/progress (heading 1) and do NOT include meeting-flow chatter. Omit if none.

(5) '**Next steps**' — a markdown table Action | Owner | Due. Include ONLY concrete tasks or promises someone actually committed to (including a verbal commitment like 'you promised you'll do it' or a stated deadline). EXCLUDE tentative musings ('we should', 'maybe', 'at some point'). Leave Owner or Due EMPTY (only spaces between the pipes) when not explicitly stated — a blank cell is never 'TBD', 'N/A', 'Unknown', a dash, or a placeholder. Omit only if there is genuinely no committed action.

CONFIDENCE RULE (applies to Questions and Feedback — the audio-derived headings): items that come from the pre-meeting notes/deck are reliable and need no marker. Items reconstructed from the meeting audio already carry a line-range cite. If such an item was garbled, half-inaudible, or you are inferring intent rather than quoting, additionally append ' ⚠️ (verify)' to it. Do NOT flag notes-based content. The goal is that a reader can trust everything without a ⚠️ and only re-check what has one.

COMPLETENESS CHECK before you finish: scan the notes AND the transcript and count every distinct project or work-stream, INCLUDING any that lacked a clean name; the number of '###' subsections you output must match that count. Dropping a work-stream because it had no tidy name, came from a separate document, or seemed minor is the single most common failure of this task — do not do it. Produce a subsection for EVERY distinct project or work-stream. End immediately after the last project's final heading — no closing sentence or sign-off.

sections.title: Open Questions & Follow-ups
sections.instruction: A single roll-up table of EVERY question or unresolved item left open in the meeting — pulled from all projects above, plus any general one. This is the follow-up checklist: nothing raised should be lost. One item per row, paraphrased. Use the same project name as the source subsection; leave the Project cell blank (nothing between the pipes) if it wasn't tied to a project. Include genuinely-open items only — those answered in the meeting do not belong here. Carry the ' ⚠️ (verify)' marker if the underlying item was audio-derived and unclear. If every question was answered, write the single line 'No open questions.' and nothing else.

sections.title: Cross-Cutting Feedback
sections.instruction: Feedback, directives, coaching, or decisions NOT tied to a single project — process, professional conduct, communication, cross-project prioritization, reporting lines, team logistics, budgets. These are usually the manager's recurring themes across the meeting; state each once even if it was triggered by a specific project's discussion, and note the trigger briefly. One concrete point per bullet, paraphrased, no named internal speakers, with a line-range cite; append ' ⚠️ (verify)' if audio-derived and unclear. OMIT this entire section if there was none — do not write 'None' or 'N/A'.

sections.title: Accuracy & Confidence Notes
sections.instruction: A short bulleted list making the review's own uncertainty explicit, so the reader knows exactly what to double-check. Include: (a) proper nouns that were probably misheard in the audio (mark them '[?]'), (b) any project whose attribution was ambiguous (a segment that could belong to two projects), (c) stretches of the meeting that were too garbled to transcribe reliably and may be missing content, and (d) any figure or claim taken from audio rather than the notes that you are unsure about. Keep it to the genuinely-uncertain items — this is not a disclaimer, it is a targeted verify-list. If the source material was clean and you are confident throughout, write the single line 'No significant uncertainty — status is from the notes and the audio was clear.'
